doc.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001

title: The shout chorus, Brazil and Wayne Shorter
summary: She questions conventions like the shout chorus and describes Brazil's music as part of life, quoting Miles via Wayne Shorter.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: It does. It’s wonderful to hear. It’s really innovative I think. I know what you mean like, you know, you get used to putting your shout chorus three quarters of the way through and, what’s going to happen at the solo, put a background after the solo.

Or that there even is a shout chorus, you know? It’s like what is a shout chorus and why? Hasn’t there been music written for centuries and in different cultures and nobody had a shout chorus. Why in jazz do we always have to have a God damn shout chorus? That’s kind of how I feel. Sometimes I hear large ensemble jazz music, so you know if you think about music, just — like I went to Brazil, you know that probably ‘cause I talked about that hang gliding piece. But I went to Brazil and one of the powerful things in Brazil was that [phone ringing] one of the powerful things in Brazil was that in Brazil music feels just synonymous with the life. Everybody makes music a part of their life. Music isn’t something you go to the conservatory for, that they have a building for, that they have funding for. Music is something that makes life tolerable. It’s a valve for releasing and creating beauty out of something that’s sometimes miserable or sometimes beautiful or whatever. But it’s an expression that everybody uses. That don’t know what bar lines are and what a four-bar phrase is. They sing in a phrase that they feel. And all the other stuff of writing it down and analyzing it is just a means to kind of put that into place. But music is the most natural thing in the world. And sometimes I think at school we make it the most complex thing in the world and it shouldn’t be. And to me music should speak — actually I met Wayne Shorter when I was in Brazil. And he said that Miles used to say he liked music that doesn’t sound like music. And I was like hallelujah. Me too.
